## Current Issue — Vol. 7 No. 3 (2026)

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center;margin:2rem 0;">
  <a href="https://ippr.in/index.php/ippr/issue/view/36" target="_blank">
    <img src="https://ippr.in/public/journals/1/cover_issue_36_en_US.png" alt="IPPR Vol. 7 No. 3 (2026) Cover" style="max-width:350px;width:100%;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:0 4px 16px rgba(0,0,0,0.12);">
  </a>
</div>
```

This special issue on Indian perspectives on China policy opens with Sarda and Ranade's analysis of China's state-directed transformation of higher education, which theorises a concentration paradox - elite targeting with fiscal restraint outperforming broad expenditure expansion. Mishra and Rishi examine India's economic and strategic entanglement with China, arguing that a multi-alignment strategy combining defensive diplomacy with supply-chain diversification best preserves strategic autonomy. Vaishnav traces the political economy of Nathu La Pass border trade, finding that regulatory restrictions rather than weak demand have suppressed formal trade and fuelled informal exchange, and calls for calibrated reform. Kumar assesses China's 2023-2025 export controls on gallium and germanium, concluding that despite sharp price volatility, Beijing failed to secure lasting leverage as the United States diversified suppliers and built domestic capability. Finally, Yanamandra's review article analyses Bambawale et al.'s Rising to the China Challenge alongside Kewalramani's Taming the Dragon, tracing how India's China strategy has moved from a framework of strategic patience to detailed operational tools across military, trade, diplomatic, and institutional domains.
